candidates.statement: The purpose of this guidance is to assist industry in developing data and obtaining information 20 needed to support approval of drug products in pediatric populations. 2 This guidance addresses 21 selected clinical, scientific, and ethical issues regarding the development of drugs for pediatric 22 use when such drugs are subject to the Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA) 3 and/or the Best 23 Pharmaceuticals for Children Act (BPCA). 4 In 2010, the Biologics Price Competition and 24 Innovation Act of 2009 extended provisions of the BPCA to biological products. 5
candidates.context: This guidance does not address the clinical development of drugs that are not subject to either 27 PREA or the BPCA. This guidance, along with the draft guidance for industry Pediatric Drug 28 Development: Regulatory Considerations — Complying With the Pediatric Research Equity Act 29

candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 41 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 42 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 43 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 44 not required. 45

candidates.statement: Under PREA, a pediatric assessment must contain data, gathered using appropriate formulations 103 for each age group for which the assessment is required, that are adequate to assess the safety 104 and effectiveness of the drug for the claimed indications in all relevant pediatric subpopulations, 105 and that support dosing and administration for each pediatric subpopulation for which the drug is 106 safe and effective. 19 If the course of the disease and the effects of the drug are sufficiently 107 similar in adults and pediatric patients, FDA may determine that pediatric effectiveness can be 108 extrapolated from adequate and well-controlled studies in adult subjects. 20

candidates.statement: It is important to note the distinction between the scope of the studies requested under the BPCA 159 and those required under PREA. FDA’s authority to issue a WR extends to the use of an active 160 moiety for indications that may produce health benefits in the pediatric population, regardless of 161 whether the indications have been previously approved in adults. 32 Under PREA, pediatric 162 assessments are required only for those indications included in the pending (or approved) 163 application. 33 To qualify for pediatric exclusivity, the pediatric studies conducted to satisfy the 164 requirements of PREA must be the subject of a WR and satisfy all other requirements for 165 pediatric exclusivity under the BPCA. 34 As discussed in the draft regulatory considerations 166 guidance, FDA does not expect to issue WRs solely for studies or planned studies that are 167 required under PREA. For more detailed information regarding WRs for pediatric studies and 168 PPSRs, see the draft Regulatory Considerations guidance. 35
candidates.context: FDA may issue a WR for pediatric studies either in response to a proposed pediatric study 153 request (PPSR) or at the initiative of FDA. A PPSR describes the studies the applicant proposes 154 to conduct. The procedures for qualifying for exclusivity and the protections to which that 155 exclusivity attaches are described in more detail in the draft Regulatory Considerations 156 guidance. 31

candidates.statement: In general, principles that guide pediatric drug development do not differ greatly from the 187 principles that apply to drugs developed for adults. Before initiating a development program in 188 pediatric populations, applicants should consider the condition(s) to be investigated, the drug 189 under study, and the pediatric subpopulation(s) for whom such a drug would represent a 190 meaningful therapeutic option. 191
candidates.context: IV. SCIENTIFIC CONSIDERATIONS FOR PEDIATRIC DRUG DEVELOPMENT 39 185 The information needed to approve a drug for pediatric use includes data from nonclinical 193 studies, and clinical dosing, safety, and effectiveness information. 40 Applicants should consider 194 whether efficacy could be partially or fully extrapolated from studies in adults or other pediatric 195 populations (see section IV.B., Pediatric Extrapolation). Finally, applicants should determine 196 whether existing data from adult human studies or animal disease models can be used to support 197 both the safety and preliminary effectiveness of the drug sufficiently to initiate pediatric studies. 198 If such information does not exist, applicants should plan and initiate necessary studies to obtain 199 this information. 200

candidates.statement: Well-designed early phase dosing studies are critical to a successful pediatric development 329 program. Inadequate dosing studies in the past have contributed to failed efficacy studies and 330 have delayed or prevented approval in pediatric age groups. Modeling and simulation, when 331 appropriate, should be used to inform dose selection and/or trial design. Confirmatory PK 332 studies may be critical, particularly in younger children, in whom dosing is not necessarily 333 predictable based on the experience in adult or adolescents. 334

candidates.statement: Safety information from adult human studies and animal models may provide preliminary 382 information regarding the expected safety profile of a drug in pediatric populations, but safety 383 information from administration of the drug to children is almost always needed to establish 384 safety in the pediatric populations. Adverse effects of a drug in pediatric populations may not be 385 predictable based on the adult experience, particularly adverse effects related to behavior, 386 cognition, or growth. Nonetheless, pediatric safety information that is available from different 387 formulations of a drug, or from other closely related drugs within the same class, as appropriate, 388 should be reviewed. In addition, because some effects may be measurable only in children of a 389 certain age or maturity level, long-term follow-up studies, particularly for drugs tested in 390 neonates, infants or young children, may be needed to assess the effects of the drug. 52 If 391 appropriate, potential risks of the drug should be assessed by age group. If there is an approved 392 risk evaluation and mitigation strategy for a drug that is already marketed for use in the adult 393 population, sponsors should assess what steps should be taken to mitigate risk in the pediatric 394 population. Pharmacovigilance programs developed to assess known or potential safety signals 395 in adult subjects should also include pediatric subjects, when appropriate. 396

candidates.statement: FDA recognizes that in some cases conducting clinical studies in pediatric populations may be 404 challenging, and study approaches commonly used to generate data in adult populations may not 405 be feasible. Pediatric ethical issues, vulnerabilities particular to the study population, limited 406 number of children available for participation in a study, difficulty in developing age- 407 appropriate endpoints, limited availability of validated patient-reported outcome measurements, 408 the potential need to use surrogate endpoints, the potential need for alternative study designs, 409 and other factors may pose unique challenges in the development of protocols for clinical 410 studies in pediatric populations. 411

candidates.statement: Applicants should consider initiation of pediatric studies during the adult development program 427 if sufficient data on the safety and potential benefit of a drug already exist (e.g., from a 428 previously approved indication, or a different formulation). For many drugs with little previous 429 human exposure, the initial phase of pediatric development (i.e., phase 1) might begin after the 430 adult phase 2 and/or 3 studies have established evidence of a sufficient prospect of direct benefit 431 to justify exposing pediatric populations to the risks of the drug. Dosing, safety, and 432 effectiveness studies may then be conducted in pediatric populations concurrently with the 433 effectiveness trial in adult subjects. 59

candidates.statement: FDA recognizes that in certain cases, scientific and ethical considerations dictate that pediatric 448 studies should not begin until after adequate safety and efficacy data are available in adult 449 subjects; for example, where a drug has not shown any advantage over other approved drugs in 450 the class, the therapeutic gain is likely to be low, and the risks of exposing pediatric subjects to 451 the new drug may not be justified until the drug’s safety profile is better established in adult 452 subjects. In these cases, the applicant can request a deferral of required pediatric studies (see 453 section III. A., PREA). However, if substantial pediatric use may be anticipated after the drug is 454 approved for use in adults, early initiation of pediatric studies should be considered. 455

candidates.statement: When drugs may be appropriate for use in the neonatal population, special consideration should 490 be given to the timing of neonatal clinical studies relative to studies in older populations. The 491 failure to study neonates before approval in older children and/or adults has meant that drugs are 492 often used in neonates without adequate information about dosing, safety, or effectiveness. 493 Unless previous animal or human data exist to suggest that use of a drug should not be studied in 494 the neonatal population because of safety concerns, FDA recommends that applicants consider 495
candidates.context: As a result of increasing attention to the lack of high-quality data for the use of drugs in 482 neonates, several provisions in the BPCA and PREA address clinical development in neonates. 483 For example, if FDA issues a WR that does not include a request to study a drug in neonates, the 484 BPCA requires that FDA “include a statement describing the rationale for not requesting studies 485 in neonates.” 63 In addition, when pediatric assessments are required under PREA, applicants are 486 required to submit assessments that are adequate to assess safety and effectiveness for the 487 claimed indications in all relevant pediatric age groups, which may include neonates. 64 62 Additional information can be found in the guidance for industry General Clinical Pharmacology Considerations for Neonatal Studies for Drugs and Biological Products .

In general, such studies should be undertaken at the same time as studies in older 497 pediatric populations, unless efficacy or safety data from older pediatric populations are 498 necessary before initiation of studies in the neonatal population. Uncertainties regarding 499 potential developmental or neurocognitive effects of a drug on the neonatal population generally 500 are not adequate justification for failing to study such effects concurrently with other pediatric 501 populations.
